name: The sixty-three Nāyaṉmārs and the nine groups of devotees

definitions.definition: The canonical company of Śiva's devotees: 63 individual saints and 9 groups (tokai aṭiyār), first listed in Cuntarar's Tiruttoṇṭattokai (Tēvāram 7.39), expanded by Nampi Āṇṭār Nampi and told at length in Cēkkiḻār's Periya Purāṇam; their images stand in Tamil Śiva temples and their days are kept as festivals. Their stories teach that love and service of Śiva and his devotees, not birth, learning or rite, win his grace; they include kings, brahmins, merchants, farmers, a hunter, a potter, a washerman, a fisherman, an outcaste, women and a former Buddhist.

members: (groups) Tillaivāḻ antaṇar — the brahmins of Tillai
Poyyaṭimai illāta pulavar — poets without false servitude
Pattarāyp paṇivār — those who bow as devotees
Paramaṉaiyē pāṭuvār — those who sing only of the Supreme
Cittattaic civaṉpālē vaittār — those who fixed their minds on Śiva
Tiruvārūrp piṟantār — those born in Tiruvārūr
Muppōtum tirumēṉi tīṇṭuvār — those who touch the holy image thrice daily (the priests)
Muḻuniṟu pūciya muṉivar — sages smeared wholly with ash
Appālum aṭicārntār — those beyond, who reached his feet
notes: Order follows the Periya Purāṇam as usually given (moderate confidence); the nine groups' names are given at moderate confidence.

name: Pati, paśu, pāśa — the Lord, the bound soul, the bonds

definitions.definition: The three eternal, irreducible categories (padārtha): Śiva, the countless souls, and the bonds (mala, karma, māyā). None is created; souls are not parts or appearances of Śiva; bonds are real.
Mupporuḷ ('the three realities') — pati, pacu, pācam; the Civañāṉa Pōtam's twelve sūtras prove and define each, then give the means and fruit.

relations.note: Kashmir non-dualism derives all categories from Śiva's consciousness; the Siddhānta keeps three
the Siddhānta denies that soul and bonds are superimposed on one reality

definitions.definition: Āṇava (innate, one, beginningless), kārma (the stream of deeds) and māyīya (the bond of māyā's products); each a real substance.
Mummalam: āṇavam, kaṉmam, māyai — eternal; in release their power is quelled, not their existence ended.

relations.note: the three plus māyeya and tirodhāna

definitions.definition: Aintu malam: āṇavam, kaṉmam, māyai, māyēyam (the products of māyā) and tirōtāyi (Śiva's concealing power, called a mala by figure).
Sanskrit lists give four or five bonds: mala, karma, māyā, rodha-śakti, and for souls of the pure worlds bindu (vaindava) — enumeration varies.

name: The three classes of souls (sakala, pralayākala, vijñānākala)

definitions.definition: Souls classed by their bonds: sakala (three bonds), pralayākala (mala and karma), vijñānākala (mala only); subdivided by the ripeness of mala.
Tirumantiram: souls of three kinds, with one, two or three malas.

Siddhānta form: five pure tattvas (Śiva/nāda, Śakti/bindu, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, Śuddhavidyā) evolved from bindu (pure māyā), not from Śiva; seven vidyā-tattvas (māyā, kalā, vidyā, rāga, kāla, niyati, puruṣa); twenty-four ātma-tattvas (prakṛti with the guṇas, buddhi, ahaṅkāra, manas, ten organs, five subtle and five gross elements). Placement of details (e.g. a separate guṇa-tattva) varies among texts.
Tattuvam 36 (5 civa, 7 vittai, 24 āṉma), which the soul must see as not-self (tattva-rūpa, -darśana, -śuddhi); expanded to 96 in Tamil lists.

relations.note: Sāṃkhya's 25 are the lower range of the 36
in the Siddhānta the tattvas are pāśa (products of bindu and māyā), not Śiva's self-manifestation

definitions.definition: Emission, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment, grace — performed by Śiva through his power, all for the souls' release; concealment ripens mala, withdrawal gives rest.
Aintoḻil, enacted in Naṭarāja's dance: drum, fearless hand, fire, planted foot, raised foot.

name: The dance of Naṭarāja and the Chidambaram tradition

definitions.definition: Śiva dances the ānanda-tāṇḍava in the hall of Chidambaram (the 'space of consciousness'), witnessed by Patañjali and Vyāghrapāda; the dance is the five acts, the raised foot being grace; Chidambaram is also the heart within the body.
Śiva as dancer in the cremation ground (Kāraikkāl Ammaiyār) and in the golden hall of Tillai (Tēvāram, Tiruvicaippā, Tirumantiram's ninth tantra).

name: The three causes of the world

definitions.definition: Śiva is the efficient cause (nimitta), māyā (and bindu) the material cause (upādāna), Śiva's power the instrumental cause (sahakārin); Śiva does not transform.

name: The two material causes: bindu (pure māyā) and māyā

definitions.definition: Bindu (mahāmāyā, śuddhamāyā) produces the pure universe, the bodies of pure beings and sound; māyā (aśuddhamāyā) produces the impure universe; prakṛti with the three guṇas arises within the māyic range.
Śiva creates the pure universe (śuddhādhvan) directly from bindu, and delegates the impure (from māyā) to Ananta, first of the Vidyeśvaras.

Ananta, Sūkṣma, Śivottama, Ekanetra, Ekarudra, Trimūrti, Śrīkaṇṭha and Śikhaṇḍin: vijñānākala souls raised to office in the pure universe, who act on Śiva's behalf and are liberated at the end of their office.

Śiva has no body of māyā; for worship and grace he is given a body of mantras — the five brahma-mantras (Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, Sadyojāta) as his faces and the six limb-mantras — made of the pure śakti; the mantras themselves are conscious beings in office.
Na-ma-śi-vā-ya, read as concealment, mala, Śiva, grace, soul; the order of the letters maps the soul's path from bondage to Śiva; meditated as the means of purification (Civañāṉa Pōtam 9).
Namaccivāya as the devotee's refuge and the essence of the Vedas (Tēvāram, Tiruvācakam).

name: The four pādas: caryā, kriyā, yoga, jñāna

definitions.definition: Every Āgama has four sections (vidyā/jñāna, kriyā, yoga, caryā); as a path, the initiate's conduct, ritual, yoga and knowledge.
Four successive stages, each containing all four in miniature (caryā-in-caryā etc.), with fruits sālokya, sāmīpya, sārūpya, sāyujya; the four paths of servant, son, friend and the true path.

relations.note: the textual quarters of an Āgama and the four stages share names

name: The four liberations (sālokya, sāmīpya, sārūpya, sāyujya)

definitions.definition: Dwelling in Śiva's world, nearness, sameness of form, and union — the first three 'station-liberations' (patamutti), only the fourth final.

relations.note: Vaiṣṇava lists add sārṣṭi and some reject sāyujya

name: The four mārgas of the samayācāryas

definitions.definition: Dāsa-mārga (Appar, caryā), satputra-mārga (Campantar, kriyā), sakhā-mārga (Cuntarar, yoga), san-mārga (Māṇikkavācakar, jñāna).
Tattva-rūpa, tattva-darśana, tattva-śuddhi; ātma-rūpa, ātma-darśana, ātma-śuddhi; śiva-rūpa, śiva-darśana, śiva-yoga, śiva-bhoga.
Āṇava mala, one with many powers, ripens through embodied experience and Śiva's concealing power until it is ready to be removed; then śaktipāta.
Malaparipākam, with iruviṉaiyoppu, is the condition for the descent of grace.

name: The balance of the two deeds (iruviṉaiyoppu)

definitions.definition: When good and bad karma come to balance and the soul regards both alike, and āṇava is ripe, grace descends and the guru appears.
The descent of Śiva's grace-power on a ripe soul, marked by signs such as devotion and the wish for release; it qualifies for dīkṣā.
Catti nipātam in four grades suited to caryā, kriyā, yoga and jñāna.
Aruḷ is Śiva's own power, always with the soul like light with the eye, embodied as the guru; liberation is by grace alone, the soul's effort being itself grace-enabled.
The Lord's grace protects in every danger and 'took me as his own' — the devotee's whole hope.
To souls who know only human forms Śiva appears in human form as the guru (as a hunter uses a decoy deer), or teaches from within to the more advanced; the guru is to be served as Śiva.
In initiation the ācārya becomes Śiva by ritual identification; Śiva's power acts through him.

relations.note: shared idea of the guru as the divine

name: The inner and outer lineages of teachers

definitions.definition: Akaccantāṉam (inner): Nandi, Sanatkumāra, Satyajñānadarśin, Parañcōti; puṟaccantāṉam (outer): Meykaṇṭār, Aruṇanti, Maṟaiñāṉa Campantar, Umāpati; the ātīṉams descend from Umāpati's disciples.

The freed soul becomes 'a Śiva': its own omniscience and omnipotence, covered since beginningless time, are manifested; it is equal to Śiva, not identical with him, and does not perform the five cosmic acts.

relations.note: the Tamil school stresses inseparability and enjoyment rather than equal powers

definitions.definition: Non-duality means non-separation (ananya), not identity: the Lord is one with souls, other than them, and together with them — as the vowel 'a' in all letters, the soul in the body, the eye's light with the sun's. In release the soul, its malas powerless, abides in Śiva enjoying his bliss, neither lost nor equal as a second agent.

relations.note: rejects identity and the unreality of the world

definitions.definition: The soul is neither Real (like Śiva) nor unreal (like the changing world) but between, taking the nature of what it joins; it knows only when made to know.
Kēvalam: the soul alone with āṇava, without instruments, like darkness; cakalam: embodied with the three malas; cuttam: purified by grace.

name: The five states (avasthā) in the Siddhānta

definitions.definition: Waking, dream, deep sleep, the fourth and beyond-the-fourth, through which the embodied soul passes; the Tamil commentators place them at the brow, throat, heart, navel and root with decreasing numbers of instruments (35, 25, 3, 2, 1 — low confidence).

name: The eight qualities of the Lord (eṇkuṇam)

definitions.definition: Self-dependence, pure body, natural understanding, omniscience, natural freedom from bonds, boundless grace, infinite power, boundless bliss (from the Āgamas, used to gloss Kuṟaḷ 9).
Four formless (Śiva, Śakti, Nāda, Bindu), one form-formless (Sadāśiva, the liṅga), and four with form (Maheśvara, Rudra, Viṣṇu, Brahmā) — the one Śiva appearing for worship.

name: The Siddhānta doxography of rival schools

definitions.definition: Rival doctrines are ranked in circles — outermost (Lokāyata, Buddhists, Jains…), outer (Vedic darśanas, Māyāvāda, Pāñcarātra…), inner-outer (Pāśupata, Kāpālika and other Śaiva sects), and inner (Śaiva views close to the Siddhānta) — each refuted in turn.

notes: Four groups of six are traditionally counted; membership lists low confidence.

name: Aṟam, poruḷ, iṉpam — the Kuṟaḷ's three aims

definitions.definition: The Kuṟaḷ is 'Muppāl', in three books on virtue, wealth and love; release (vīṭu) is taught within virtue (renunciation, truth, desire's end).
Samaya, viśeṣa and nirvāṇa dīkṣā, then consecrations (ācāryābhiṣeka, sādhakābhiṣeka); nirvāṇa-dīkṣā with or without 'seed'.
Seven modes: by look, touch, word, thought, scripture, yoga and the fire rite.
Samayin, putraka, sādhaka (seeker of powers, bubhukṣu) and ācārya; the mumukṣu is liberated at death.
After grace and knowledge the body continues by prārabdha; the jīvanmukta acts as Śiva's servant among devotees, untouched by deeds.
The initiate liberated by nirvāṇa-dīkṣā is released at death; the body continues until prārabdha is exhausted.
Cañcitam (stored), pirārattam (begun, which forms this body) and ākāmiyam (being made): dīkṣā and grace burn the first, the second is exhausted by experience, the third does not bind the freed.
